summary.text: 弟 commonly means ‘younger brother’ and also ‘junior.’ Early forms have been interpreted as a binding wrapped around an implement, but that reading does not by itself explain how the graph came to mean a sibling.

formation.text: Pictographic: the proposed picture shows a binding around an implement. The implement is variously identified as a shaft or peg. The further proposal that orderly binding suggested sequence and then sibling rank is an interpretation; the evidence does not establish that sequence of meanings.

components.text: The graph is treated as one picture of a binding around an implement, rather than as a proven combination of current components. The implement is interpreted variously as a shaft or peg; early forms are described with an element identified as 必/柲, while some bronze forms are described with 弋. The evidence does not establish a sequence among these forms.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze forms are reported, but the evidence does not establish a continuous graphic sequence to the modern form. The Shuowen account describes successive leather bindings and says the graph follows an ancient form; this is a historical explanation, not a verified reading of the earliest picture.
In 第, 弟 serves as a phonetic component. That role belongs to 第 and does not make 弟 itself a phonosemantic compound.

uncertainties.text: The proposed implement’s spoken name is not established. Therefore, the idea that 弟 was reused for ‘younger brother’ because the object’s name sounded similar is possible but un demonstrated by the evidence here.

The early forms do not establish an early ‘younger brother’ meaning. A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟, but its exact date is unresolved; the evidence also does not establish an earlier sequence or rank use.

senses.period: Western Zhou bronze inscription evidence; exact date unresolved
senses.text: A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟. This is the earliest securely sourced sibling use in the evidence provided, but it does not show that the earliest oracle-bone forms already had this meaning.

senses.gloss: junior; younger person or lower in rank
senses.text: The character is also used for junior status and sequence or rank. The evidence does not establish when these uses began or whether one developed from the other.

senses.period: Attestations cited from a Tang poem and later literature; witness dates not checked
senses.text: In literary contexts, 弟 can serve as humble self-reference among peers. Its earliest use and path from a junior designation are unresolved; this sense does not show that the character originally meant ‘I.’
Classical citations are reported for female younger-sibling or junior uses. Their dates and relationship to the broader junior sense are unresolved.

senses.gloss: younger sibling; later narrowed in Japanese to younger male sibling
senses.period: Japanese oto use cited in 712; narrowing reported for the Edo period
senses.text: Japanese lexical history records oto for a younger person of either sex and reports that おとうと later narrowed to a younger male sibling. This is the history of Japanese words, not an explanation of the Chinese graph’s origin.

developments.text: The humble self-reference may be pragmatically related to a junior or younger-peer designation, but the pathway and earliest use are unresolved.

limitations.text: The binding-to-sequence account is an interpretation, and no independently dated sequence or rank use earlier than the sibling sense is established. A semantic chain between these senses cannot be specified.
The evidence gives separate readings and senses, including an ethical 悌-related use, but does not establish a unified development connecting them to the common sibling meaning.

overview.text: 弟 commonly means ‘younger brother’ and can also mean ‘junior.’ Its early form is interpreted as a binding around an implement, but that picture alone does not explain the sibling meaning.

components.text: Treat 弟 as one proposed picture of a binding around an implement; the object and the picture’s interpretation remain uncertain.

takeaway.text: Sound borrowing is a possible explanation for the sibling meaning, but the evidence does not establish the implement’s name or a sound match.
